config.title: Conditional Rendering with Ternary

intro.title: Conditional Rendering with Ternary
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React component that displays a personalized greeting message based on whether a user is logged in. You will learn how to use the ternary operator for conditional rendering in JSX, which allows you to show different UI elements depending on a condition. The main technologies involved are React, TypeScript, and JSX, focusing on writing clean, type-safe conditional logic. This is a fundamental pattern in React for creating dynamic and responsive user interfaces.
intro.usecase: Conditional rendering with the ternary operator is a foundational pattern for building dynamic user interfaces that respond to user input or application state. For example, in an e-commerce dashboard, you might use it to show a 'Loading...' spinner while fetching product data, then display the product list once the data arrives, or an error message if the fetch fails. It's commonly used to toggle UI elements like buttons (enabled/disabled), form validation messages (show/hide), or conditional panels in a settings menu based on user selections, making interfaces feel immediate and interactive.

objectives: Implement a ternary operator to conditionally render JSX elements based on a boolean state variable.
Apply the ternary operator to display different text content depending on a component's props.
Construct a React component that toggles UI visibility using a ternary expression with a click handler.
Configure a ternary operator to return alternative JSX structures for true and false conditions.
Update a state variable to dynamically control which branch of a ternary operator renders.
Integrate a ternary operator within JSX to conditionally apply CSS classes to an element.
Manipulate a component to render a fallback UI when data is missing using a ternary operator.

steps.title: Create the main component

import React, { useState } from 'react';

steps.title: Initialize a boolean state variable
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, declare a state variable named 'isLoggedIn' with an initial value of false, using useState.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to include the type annotation for TypeScript.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing a boolean state variable
const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now has a state variable 'isLoggedIn' initialized to false, ready to control conditional rendering.
successCriteria: The component contains a state variable declaration for 'isLoggedIn' with an initial value of false using useState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using useState with the correct syntax and type annotation for TypeScript.
steps.feedbackWrong: use useState to create a state variable named 'isLoggedIn' with an initial value of false.

steps.title: Define a handler to toggle the state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function named 'toggleLogin' that toggles the boolean value of the 'isLoggedIn' state variable.
steps.hint: Use the setter function from useState to update the state. You can toggle a boolean by setting it to the opposite of its current value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The toggleLogin function will be available to call, flipping the isLoggedIn state between true and false.
successCriteria: A function named toggleLogin is defined inside the App component, and it updates the isLoggedIn state using setIsLoggedIn.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but make sure it toggles the isLoggedIn state correctly using setIsLoggedIn.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggleLogin function is not defined correctly. Ensure it's inside the App component and updates the state.

steps.title: Add a button to trigger the toggle
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a button element with the text 'Toggle Login' and wire its onClick event to the toggleLogin handler.
steps.hint: Remember to define the toggleLogin function first if you haven't already, then add the button with onClick={toggleLogin}.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now have a button that, when clicked, toggles the isLoggedIn state between true and false.
successCriteria: A button element is present in the return statement
The button's onClick is wired to the toggleLogin handler
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly set up. Check that you've added a button element with the correct text and onClick handler.

steps.title: Introduce the ternary operator for conditional rendering
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, use a ternary operator to conditionally render a paragraph: if 'isLoggedIn' is true, show 'Welcome back!', otherwise show 'Please log in.'
steps.hint: The ternary operator syntax is: condition ? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse. Place it inside curly braces {} in your JSX.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will conditionally display different text based on the isLoggedIn state using a ternary operator.
successCriteria: A ternary operator is used to conditionally render either 'Welcome back!' or 'Please log in.' based on the isLoggedIn state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the ternary operator correctly. Check that you have both true and false branches with the correct text.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ternary operator isn't implemented correctly. Remember the syntax: condition ? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse. Both branches should return JSX elements.

steps.title: Conditionally render a user greeting
steps.instruction: In your component's JSX, add another ternary operator that conditionally renders an h2 element: if 'isLoggedIn' is true, show 'Hello, User!', otherwise show 'Guest Access'.
steps.hint: Add a new line in the return statement using the same 'isLoggedIn' state variable with a ternary operator to decide which h2 text to display.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show an h2 heading that changes between 'Hello, User!' and 'Guest Access' when the login state toggles.
successCriteria: An h2 element is rendered conditionally using a ternary operator that checks 'isLoggedIn' and displays the appropriate greeting text.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using a ternary operator with 'isLoggedIn' to render an h2 element with the correct text in both branches.
steps.feedbackWrong: The expected action was to add a ternary operator that conditionally renders an h2 element with different text based on the 'isLoggedIn' state.

steps.title: Conditionally apply CSS classes
steps.instruction: Add a <div> element that uses a ternary operator to set its className attribute to 'user-panel' when isLoggedIn is true and 'guest-panel' when false. Include placeholder text like 'User panel content' or 'Guest panel content' inside the div.
steps.hint: Use the syntax className={isLoggedIn ? 'user-panel' : 'guest-panel'} on a div element. Place it after the existing conditional paragraph.

// Conditional className example

steps.expectedOutcome: A div element appears in the UI that changes its CSS class based on the login state, demonstrating dynamic attribute assignment with ternary operators.
successCriteria: The code includes a div element with className set using a ternary operator that references isLoggedIn, with appropriate class names for true/false states and placeholder text content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using a ternary operator (condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse) to set the className attribute on a div element, with different class names for logged in vs logged out states.
steps.feedbackWrong: The div element with conditional className wasn't added correctly. Remember to use the syntax: className={isLoggedIn ? 'user-panel' : 'guest-panel'} on a div element, and include some text content inside.
